---
title: "Job B — Neutralize an Income Model"
subtitle: "Fairness on real US Census income data"
---



*Do-the-job track · Job B of 3.*

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
**See the data first** — [The Income & Fairness
Dataset](../../data/06-the-credit-dataset.qmd) shows this table's group gap and the
proxy channels (above all `occupation`) that leak `sex` even when it's dropped.
:::

The real deliverable: take an income-scoring model that *drops* the protected
attribute, show it still leaks, then neutralize it and report the group gap before
and after.  The data is real — the US Census **ACSIncome** table (`sex` protected,
`income_high` target, real proxy features).

---

## 1 · The Gap, and the Proxy Channels

::: {#71866d26 .cell execution_count=2}
``` {.python .cell-code}
credit = datasets.load_credit()
print(f"loaded {len(credit):,} rows")
m, f = credit[credit.sex == 1], credit[credit.sex == 0]
print(f"P(high income | male)   = {m.income_high.mean():.2f}")
print(f"P(high income | female) = {f.income_high.mean():.2f}   "
      f"← gap {m.income_high.mean() - f.income_high.mean():+.2f}")
print()
for c in ["age", "education_years", "hours_per_week"]:
    print(f"corr({c:<16}, sex) = {credit[c].corr(credit.sex):+.2f}   (numeric proxy)")
print("occupation               : categorical — the strong channel (see the data page)")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
loaded 30,000 rows
P(high income | male)   = 0.47
P(high income | female) = 0.35   ← gap +0.12

corr(age             , sex) = +0.01   (numeric proxy)
corr(education_years , sex) = -0.06   (numeric proxy)
corr(hours_per_week  , sex) = +0.19   (numeric proxy)
occupation               : categorical — the strong channel (see the data page)
```
:::
:::


The numeric features barely correlate with `sex`.  The leak rides mostly on
**`occupation`**, which the data page showed is heavily sex-segregated.

## 2 · Drop `sex`, and Watch It Leak

Build a score from the proxy features only — numeric features plus a one-hot of
`occupation`, with `sex` never an input — then measure the **group gap** in the
score (the difference in mean score between men and women).

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
We work on a representative 2 000-row sample (the kernel measure below builds an
$n \times n$ matrix).  We report the **group gap** rather than CKA: with a single
**binary** protected column, CKA barely registers the mean shift (it stays near
0.02 throughout).  The group gap is the sharper read here — CKA earns its keep when
$S$ is multivariate or continuous (see [Dependence](../../dependence/index.qmd)).
:::

::: {#670041cd .cell execution_count=3}
``` {.python .cell-code}
sample = credit.sample(n=2000, random_state=0).reset_index(drop=True)
num = ["age", "education_years", "hours_per_week"]
Xn = sample[num].to_numpy(dtype=float)
Xn = (Xn - Xn.mean(0)) / Xn.std(0)
Xocc = pd.get_dummies(sample["occupation"]).to_numpy(dtype=float)   # the proxy
X = np.column_stack([Xn, Xocc])
y = sample["income_high"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
S = sample["sex"].to_numpy(dtype=float)

# Composite baseline score from the legitimate features (sex excluded).
Xa = np.column_stack([X, np.ones(len(X))])
w, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(Xa, y, rcond=None)
score = Xa @ w

gap = score[S == 1].mean() - score[S == 0].mean()
data_gap = m.income_high.mean() - f.income_high.mean()
print(f"score group gap (sex dropped) = {gap:+.3f}")
print(f"  → about {gap / data_gap:.0%} of the data's {data_gap:+.2f} income gap, "
      f"leaked through proxies")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
score group gap (sex dropped) = +0.046
  → about 38% of the data's +0.12 income gap, leaked through proxies
```
:::
:::


Even with `sex` dropped, men get a systematically higher score — the proxies
carried it through.

::: {#cell-fig-jobB-leak .cell execution_count=4}
``` {.python .cell-code}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 4.0))
for g, col, name in [(0, WARM, "women"), (1, COOL, "men")]:
    ax.hist(score[S == g], bins=30, density=True, alpha=0.55, color=col, label=name)
    ax.axvline(score[S == g].mean(), color=col, lw=2, ls="--")
ax.set_xlabel("baseline score"); ax.set_ylabel("density")
ax.set_title(f"Score leaks the dropped attribute · group gap = {gap:+.3f}",
             fontsize=12)
ax.legend(fontsize=9, frameon=False); despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Baseline score distribution by group (sex dropped). The dashed group means are offset: despite never seeing sex, the score hands men a higher value, reproducing a large share of the income gap through occupation and hours.](lab-jobB-neutralize-credit_files/figure-html/fig-jobb-leak-output-1.png){#fig-jobb-leak width=884 height=465}
:::
:::


## 3 · Neutralize, and Sweep the Trade-Off

`fair_fit` re-fits `income_high` from the score while penalizing dependence on
`sex`: at $\mu = 0$ it is free to use the sex-aligned signal (the worst case); as
$\mu$ grows it ridge-removes that component, driving the group gap to zero.

::: {#0e74410a .cell execution_count=5}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def group_gap(pred):
    return pred[S == 1].mean() - pred[S == 0].mean()

def utility(pred):
    return float(np.corrcoef(pred, y)[0, 1])  # correlation with the target

sweep = [0.0, 0.5, 2.0, 8.0, 20.0]
print(f"{'μ':>6}{'group gap':>12}{'CKA':>9}{'utility':>10}")
print("-" * 37)
gaps, ckas, utils = [], [], []
for mu in sweep:
    p = fair_fit(score, y, S, mu=mu)
    g, c, u = group_gap(p), cka_rbf(p, S), utility(p)
    gaps.append(g); ckas.append(c); utils.append(u)
    print(f"{mu:>6g}{g:>+12.3f}{c:>9.3f}{u:>10.3f}")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
     μ   group gap      CKA   utility
-------------------------------------
     0      +0.105    0.017     0.587
   0.5      +0.042    0.004     0.583
     2      +0.015    0.002     0.580
     8      +0.004    0.002     0.578
    20      +0.002    0.002     0.577
```
:::
:::


::: {#cell-fig-jobB-neutralize .cell execution_count=6}
``` {.python .cell-code}
fig, (axL, axR) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11.5, 4.3))

axL.plot(sweep, np.abs(gaps), "-o", c=CRASH, lw=2.2)
axL.set_xlabel("neutrality weight μ"); axL.set_ylabel("|group gap| in mean score")
axL.set_title("The group gap closes", fontsize=12)
despine(axL)

axR.plot(np.abs(gaps), utils, "-o", c=COOL, lw=2.2)
for mu, gx, uy in zip(sweep, np.abs(gaps), utils):
    axR.annotate(f"μ={mu:g}", (gx, uy), textcoords="offset points",
                 xytext=(6, 5), fontsize=9, color=INK)
axR.set_xlabel("|group gap|  →  less fair")
axR.set_ylabel("utility (corr with income)")
axR.set_title("Utility vs the group gap", fontsize=12)
despine(axR)

fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Left: the group gap collapses as the neutrality weight μ grows. Right: the frontier — utility (correlation with income) versus the group gap. Neutralisation here is nearly free: the gap falls almost to zero while utility barely moves.](lab-jobB-neutralize-credit_files/figure-html/fig-jobb-neutralize-output-1.png){#fig-jobb-neutralize width=1361 height=502}
:::
:::


::: {.callout-tip}
## The Deliverable
Report the *operating point*, not a single model: "at μ = … we cut the group gap
from … to …, keeping … of baseline utility."  Here the gap falls to near zero —
below even the +0.05 left by *naively dropping* `sex` — while utility drops only a
couple of percent.  Neutralising the outcome beats whacking proxies: the choice of
μ is a policy decision, and the maths only gives you the frontier.
:::

---

## Your Turn

- Add a hard-threshold view: approve where `score >= 0.5`, and tabulate approval
  and false-decline rates per group at μ = 0 vs μ = 8.
- Which channel leaks most?  Drop the `occupation` one-hot and re-fit the baseline
  — the gap shrinks but does **not** vanish (hours-worked still carries some sex).
  The leak is distributed, which is why neutralising the *outcome* beats whacking
  proxies one by one.
